newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian shares jump as Creditanstalt battle ends.
newsitem.headline: Austrian shares jump as Creditanstalt battle ends.

text.p: Austrian shares jumped on Monday as investors welcomed the sale of Creditanstalt to Bank Austria despite doubts over the potential for synergies in the formation of a new Alpine superbank.

Market leader Bank Austria took control of its main competitor Creditanstalt-Bankverein after leaders of Austria's divided Social Democrat-conservative government coalition struck a last-minute deal early on Sunday morning.

The Vienna bourse's ATX index of 21 blue chips jumped more than two percent in reaction to the agreement, which was widely seen as having averted the imminent danger of a government collapse just one year after the country's last snap-election.
"The fact that political stability has been secured brought investors back to Vienna," one trader said.
Investors scrambled to pick up shares of Creditanstalt, pushing its preference stock up 16.8 schillings ($1.5) to 495 and the bank's common shares up nine schillings to 729.50.
Bank Austria, which on Sunday said it expected its earnings per share to double over the next five years as a result of the deal, was up five schillings at 406.

At Creditanstalt's headquarters, the mood remained glum. Non-executive supervisory board chairman Walter Fremuth offered his resignation to the bank's new majority owner and said it was up to the executive board to determine whether it wanted to stay on or put up their jobs for grabs as well.
Analysts said the 17.2 billion schilling deal to create the new banking giant was likely to be followed by a flurry of takeovers in the country's traditionally overcrowded financial scene.

"It is often the case in Europe that where there is one big merger others follow as the competitive environment changes. We have seen it in Holland recently and in Britain," said James Alexander, banking analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.

Experts said it would force other Austrian banks to seek out partners in order to shore up their market position or risk being swept away by a tide of increased competition at the start of a single European currency.
The link-up of Austria's two biggest banks will create a financial powerhouse to rank among Europe's top 30 and almost completely dominate the domestic scene.

With total assets of some 1,400 billion schillings, the combined bank will control 80 percent of Vienna bourse trading, half of the Austria's export financing and 70 percent of the country's commercial banking.

But details of how the merged bank will realise promised synergies remained sketchy. "The general inefficiency within the Austrian banking system makes me very dubious about whether they can actually get the synergy gains they need," said Victoria Maxwell, Austria analyst at James Capel in London.

Under strong political pressure to make the sale of the establishment bank to what is effectively a Social-Democrat controlled rival more digestible to the conservatives, Bank Austria agreed to keep on all of Creditanstalt's 9,800 employees and guarantee the bank's independence for five years.
Bank Austria itself agreed to be taken out of public control successively and to see the City of Vienna's influence of the bank reduced.
That move could endanger its triple-A rating, which was effectively secured by the municipal guarantee of Bank Austria's present and future liabilities. ($ = 11.13 Austrian Schillings)
